cases.limit: Neither the coefficient nor the temperature difference is a verified specification or local weather assumption.
cases.summary: Apply the temperature difference and coefficient to the corresponding reference quantity. The example gives 455 W. Do not apply a power coefficient indiscriminately to voltage or whole-system financial benefits.

cases.title: A simplified resource-to-energy illustration
cases.given: Use a hypothetical 4 kW rating, 4 equivalent full-sun hours and a single assumed overall energy factor of 0.8 for this example.
cases.steps: Illustrative energy = 4 × 4 × 0.8 = 12.8 kWh.
cases.meaning: This is a deliberately compressed model showing why rated power, integrated resource and a stated factor are different inputs. A site forecast requires appropriate data and a clearer treatment of system conditions.
cases.limit: Four sun hours and the 0.8 factor are not published assumptions for Antigua, Dominica or a company package.
cases.summary: The 4 kW array, four equivalent sun hours and 0.8 factor are teaching assumptions. They explain the calculation, not a local generation promise or the performance of a company package.

cases.title: Sequential efficiency stages are multiplied
cases.given: A hypothetical path has one stage at 95% efficiency followed by a different stage at 90%, with 10 kWh entering the first stage.
cases.steps: Combined fraction = 0.95 × 0.9 = 0.855. Output = 10 × 0.855 = 8.55 kWh.
cases.meaning: The second stage acts on the output of the first. The calculation should not be used if a quoted round-trip figure already includes both stages, because that would count the same losses twice.
cases.limit: These assumed percentages do not describe any offered equipment.
cases.summary: Sequential conversion stages act one after another, producing 8.55 kWh in this example. If a total efficiency already includes those stages, do not deduct them again.

cases.title: Self-consumption and self-sufficiency use different denominators
cases.given: Over the same hypothetical period without storage, PV generates 20 kWh, 12 kWh is used directly at home, and total household demand is 30 kWh.
cases.steps: Direct solar self-consumption = 12 ÷ 20 = 60%. On-site contribution to total demand = 12 ÷ 30 = 40%.
cases.meaning: Both percentages can be correct because they answer different questions. The first concerns use of generation; the second concerns supply of demand. Define boundaries again if storage is included.
cases.limit: Do not describe either percentage as bill savings without the tariff and other costs.
cases.summary: The ratio 12/20 describes the fraction of generation used on site; 12/30 describes the fraction of total demand supplied by on-site solar. Neither ratio directly equals the reduction in the electricity bill.

cases.title: The incremental value of shifting surplus energy through storage
cases.given: Hypothetically, 5 kWh would otherwise be exported at 0.10 currency units/kWh. Storage later delivers 4.5 kWh that avoids purchases at 0.30 currency units/kWh.
cases.steps: Avoided purchase cost = 4.5 × 0.30 = 1.35. Forgone export value = 5 × 0.10 = 0.50. Difference = 0.85 currency units before other costs.
cases.meaning: Count the alternative use of the charging energy and the output boundary. The difference still excludes storage purchase, ageing, maintenance and any other relevant charges.
cases.limit: The example assumes export is available and gives invented prices. It does not establish a local tariff or an investment return.
cases.summary: When assessing incremental storage benefits, account for the export value forgone and the energy actually delivered after conversion losses. The illustrative prices are not local tariffs.

cases.title: A shared conversion ceiling can constrain combined sources
cases.given: An abstract example has a shared AC output ceiling of 5 kW. The current solar contribution is 4.8 kW and household demand is 6 kW. Other limits are ignored.
cases.steps: Headroom within the shared ceiling is 5 − 4.8 = 0.2 kW. Even if the battery could contribute more on its own, this example's combined path cannot exceed 5 kW.
cases.meaning: Adding independent source ratings would miss a shared bottleneck. Any remaining demand requires another supported source or a different demand arrangement; the assistant cannot infer either.
cases.limit: This is a conceptual limit example, not the wiring or operation of a specific hybrid inverter.
cases.summary: Do not simply add the separate solar and battery output ratings. If they share a path limited to 5 kW, combined output remains subject to that limit.

cases.title: Whole-project payback versus incremental battery payback
cases.given: Hypothetical solar-only cost is 20,000 currency units with annual benefit 2,000. Solar-plus-storage cost is 30,000 with annual benefit 2,400. Hold values constant and omit other costs.
cases.steps: Simple ratios are 20,000 ÷ 2,000 = 10 years and 30,000 ÷ 2,400 = 12.5 years. Incremental storage ratio is (30,000 − 20,000) ÷ (2,400 − 2,000) = 25 years.
cases.meaning: Attributing all project benefit to the battery would conceal the incremental comparison. Backup resilience is a separate customer objective that this simple money-only calculation does not value.
cases.limit: This is not a quotation, forecast, recommendation or complete investment model.
cases.summary: Evaluate storage using its additional cost and additional benefit, rather than assigning all solar benefits to the battery. Backup value is also separate from this simple-payback calculation.

cases.title: Discounting one future cash flow
cases.given: Assume a hypothetical benefit of 1,000 currency units one year from now and an illustrative discount rate of 5%.
cases.steps: Present value = 1,000 ÷ 1.05 ≈ 952.381 currency units.
cases.meaning: The example shows that cash flows at different times can be compared using an explicitly chosen financial assumption. A real analysis would need its full horizon, costs, benefits and a justified rate.
cases.limit: Five percent is not a company financing offer, a required discount rate or a prediction of inflation.
cases.summary: The discount rate is an analytical assumption that must be stated. The example's 5% is not a financing rate, inflation forecast or recommended rate for a customer's project.

cases.title: Integrating a time-based power profile
cases.given: A hypothetical trace is exactly 1.5 kW for 2 hours and 0.5 kW for 4 hours.
cases.meaning: This relationship holds for the defined intervals. A few screenshots taken during a day do not establish that power stayed constant between them. Meter or monitoring energy totals can provide a different kind of evidence.
cases.limit: Do not integrate sparse observations as if they were complete measured intervals.
cases.summary: Accumulate energy by interval only when each interval's power and duration are known. A few screenshots do not establish that power remained constant between captures.

cases.title: Full charge on a reduced capacity reference
cases.given: A hypothetical battery began with a 10 kWh energy reference. For this illustration its present relevant full-capacity reference is 90% of that original value.
cases.steps: Present full reference = 10 × 0.9 = 9 kWh.
cases.meaning: A display of full charge can refer to the current capacity while health compares with an earlier reference. The example does not define the actual manufacturer's SOC or SOH method.
cases.limit: Do not infer a replacement decision or warranty result from this invented percentage.
cases.summary: A current full-charge reading and original capacity use different reference points. This example explains the distinction between SOC and health-related capacity; it cannot determine replacement or warranty eligibility.

cases.title: Prioritising essential energy in a defined outage window
cases.given: Assume 6 kWh is already available at the load, essentials need 0.25 kW for 8 hours, and an optional load would draw 1 kW. Ignore other energy use and require the separate power limit to be satisfied.
cases.steps: Essential energy = 0.25 × 8 = 2 kWh. Remaining energy = 6 − 2 = 4 kWh, corresponding to 4 hours of the optional 1 kW load in this ideal model.
cases.meaning: A priority plan can distinguish essential service from discretionary use rather than assuming every load runs for the whole outage. Starting demand and simultaneous power remain separate questions.
cases.limit: The example is not an operational instruction, appliance recommendation or actual backup promise.
cases.summary: Calculate essential-load energy first, then examine how much optional demand the remaining energy could support. Check output and starting limits separately. The example is not an actual operating plan.
